BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS DISCIPLINARY TRIBUNAL
HPDT NO: 992/DTech18/426P
UNDER the Health Practitioners Competence
Assurance Act 2003 (“the Act”)
IN THE MATTER of a disciplinary Charge laid against a health
practitioner under Part 4 of the Act.
BETWEEN A PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT
COMMITTEE appointed by the DENTAL
COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND
Applicant
AND Mr D, registered dental technician and
registered clinical dental technician of X
Practitioner
ORDER ON APPLICATION TO WITHDRAW CHARGE
On the papers
CHAIR: Mr D Carden
Ms L Carlyon, Ms J Hearn, Mr J Egan and Mr M Smith (Members)

2
1. The Professional Conduct Committee (PCC) appointed by the Dental Council of
New Zealand has, by letter from counsel on its behalf dated 5 October 2018, sought
leave to withdraw the Charge against the practitioner in this matter.
2. The grounds for the application are that the complainant, on whose evidence the
PCC will rely to prove the Charge, has indicated clearly that she does not wish to be
further involved or to give evidence against the practitioner. It is said that she wants
to put the matter behind her. The letter referred to the complainant’s mental state
and emotional wellbeing. The PCC cannot proceed with the Charge against the
practitioner without evidence from that complainant.
3. In an email response from counsel for the practitioner dated 11 October 2018 he
agreed to withdrawal of the Charge. In a subsequent telephone conference counsel
said that the allegations would be strenuously denied by the practitioner and the
Charge would be defended.
4. The Charge against the practitioner alleges certain breach of boundary issues
extending over a significant period of time. Some of the allegations are vague as to
time and content. There is a noticeable time lapse between events giving rise to the
allegations and questions concerning on-going consultation by the complainant with
the practitioner in those circumstances.
5. In a telephone conference counsel for the PCC advised:
5.1 That there have been no other complaints against the practitioner and this has
been confirmed.
5.2 That the PCC could not proceed to try to prove the Charge and its allegations
without the evidence of the complainant.
Counsel for the practitioner said:
5.3 That the Charge was strenuously denied by him.
5.4 That there had been no previous complaints and he referred to an affidavit
filed in support of a name suppression application.
5.5 That he would certainly be wanting to cross-examine the complainant in
respect of any evidence she may give because of that denial.
5.6 That there was a stated ulterior purpose behind the initial complaint by the
complainant to the NZ Police.
5.7 That there was no issue as to costs.

3
6. The Tribunal has been faced with applications of this nature to withdraw a charge in
the past.1
7. Those decisions find that the primary question is that:
“… the Tribunal must be satisfied that the parties have no sound objection
to that course of action and that there are no outstanding public interest
issues that ought to be the subject of enquiry by the Tribunal
notwithstanding the attitude or agreement of the parties.”
8. Having considered the Charge, the ground for application and the advices from
counsel for the parties, the Tribunal concludes there is too much uncertainty about
the allegations in the Charge for them to proceed to any hearing without direct
evidence from the complainant. She would be the primary witness. The matter
could not begin to be inquired into by the Tribunal without her.
9. The Tribunal has concluded that leave should be granted to withdraw the Charge as
sought.
10. By application dated 19 October 2018 the practitioner applied for an order under
section 95 of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 prohibiting
publication of his name or any particulars of his affairs. He filed an affidavit in
support. In that affidavit he outlined his age and personal position and his
professional career spanning over 35 years. He said that the complaints in this
proceeding were the only complaints he had had in all that time. He gave detail of
his family situation and the situation of the community in which he lives and
practices.
11. Section 95 of the HPCA Act includes:
“95 Hearings to be public unless Tribunal orders otherwise
(1) Every hearing of the Tribunal must be held in public unless the
Tribunal orders otherwise under this section or unless section 97
applies.
(2) If, after having regard to the interests of any person (including,
without limitation, the privacy of any complainant) and to the public
interest, the Tribunal is satisfied that it is desirable to do so, it may
(on application by any of the parties or on its own initiative) make any
1 or more of the following orders:
1 Mr T 582/Med13/237P; Dr T 70/Med06/41D; Dr H 361/Med10/165P

4
…
(d) an order prohibiting the publication of the name, or any
particulars of the affairs, of any person.”
12. The presumption in section 95(1) of the Act that the Tribunal’s hearings shall be in
public are the primary principle and endorse the principle of open justice; but section
95(2) does give the Tribunal discretion to grant name suppression.
13. The test is whether it is “desirable” to prohibit the publication of the name or any
particulars of the affairs of the person in question and the Tribunal must consider
both:
13.1 The interest of any person and
13.2 The public interest.
14. There have been many public interest factors identified by other Tribunal decisions.
These include:
14.1 Openness and transparency of disciplinary proceedings.2
14.2 Accountability of the disciplinary process.3
14.3 Public interest in knowing the identity of a health practitioner charged with a
disciplinary offence.4
14.4 Unfairly impugning other practitioners.
15. The Tribunal has concluded in light of the authorities and taking account of
information provided that an order should be made as sought. The interests of the
practitioner, his family, his community, and the profession in that community
outweigh any public interest in having his name publicised in a context of the Charge
which has been withdrawn because of reluctance or refusal of the complainant to
give evidence to support it.
Result and orders
16. Leave is granted to the PCC to withdraw the Charge and it is withdrawn accordingly.
2 M v Police (1991) 8 CRNZ 14; R v Liddell [1995]1 NZLR 538; Lewis v Wilson & Horton Ltd. [2000] 3
NZLR 546; Director of Proceedings v I [2004] NZAR 635.
3 Director of Proceedings v Nursing Council [1999] 3 NZLR 360.
4 Director of Proceedings v Nursing Council [1999] 3 NZLR 360; F v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary
Tribunal HC Auckland AP21–SW0T 5 December 2001 per Laurenson J.

5
17. There is an order made permanently prohibiting the publication of the practitioner’s
name or any particulars of his affairs or other identifying information.
DATED at Auckland this 1st day of November 2018
